svg.title: A Halloween evening that welcomes everyone

text.tspan: Everyday English - C1 - 2026/10/30 - Essay - 01
A costume creates a playful Halloween character.
Pexels · 29225548
A Halloween evening that welcomes everyone
The decision to prepare a Halloween evening may appear ordinary, yet it exposes a recurring tension between arrangements that make life
manageable and experiences that resist being prescribed. A defensible approach combines proportionate preparation with a willingness to
reconsider whose interests a plan serves.
Preparation has value because planning the route and the costumes helps everyone stay comfortable. In the present case, we check that
costumes allow clear vision and choose a well-lit route. Such an intervention is modest, but that modesty is its strength: it removes a
foreseeable obstacle without claiming to determine the entire experience. Structure is useful to the extent that it releases attention rather than
consuming it.
That argument requires a qualification, however: clear choices make sharing treats more considerate. For instance, we keep ingredient
information available and offer a non-food option. An arrangement that appears efficient from one standpoint may impose costs elsewhere.
Listening to those affected is therefore not an optional gesture of goodwill; it supplies information without which the plan cannot be adequately
evaluated.
The resulting principle is one of proportion. Preparation deserves support when it clarifies responsibilities and protects time, while
responsiveness prevents it from hardening into an end in itself. To judge the experience well is to examine both what the arrangement
enables and what it may inadvertently exclude.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body
paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Write about an attempt to prepare a Halloween evening that did not go as planned. Explain two lessons, each supported by a specific
incident. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion.
